cmimc-2016-power-s3-01.title: Trace each string
cmimc-2016-power-s3-01.body:
The DFA stays in $q_0$ on $0$s, moves to $q_1$ on the first $1$, stays in $q_1$ on $1$s, moves to the accepting state $q_2$ on a $0$ from $q_1$, and any further letter sends it to the dead state $q_3$. So it accepts exactly the strings $0^m1^n0$ ($m\ge0$, $n\ge1$).

- $0000$: $q_0$ throughout, ends in $q_0$: **rejects**.
- $1111$: $q_0\to q_1\to q_1\to q_1\to q_1$: **rejects**.
- $0010$: $q_0,q_0,q_0\to q_1\to q_2$: **accepts**.
- $0110$: $q_0\to q_0\to q_1\to q_1\to q_2$: **accepts**.
- $0100$: $q_0\to q_0\to q_1\to q_2\to q_3$: **rejects**.

cmimc-2016-power-s3-02a.title: Interpret the states
cmimc-2016-power-s3-02a.body: $q_0$ is the start (nothing read). $q_1$ means "only $0$s so far" (a $0$ loops), $q_2$ means "only $1$s so far". From $q_1$ a $1$ leads to $q_3$, and from $q_2$ a $0$ leads to $q_3$; $q_3$ is accepting and absorbing. So a string is accepted iff it contains both symbols: it has at least one $0$ and at least one $1$ (equivalently, it is not of the form $0^m$ or $1^m$).

cmimc-2016-power-s3-02b.title: Run-length tracking
cmimc-2016-power-s3-02b.body: From $q_0$, a $0$ goes to $q_1$ and a $1$ to $q_2$. $q_1$ = "current run is a single $0$", $q_3$ = "current run is $00$"; $q_2$ = "single $1$", $q_4$ = "run $11$". A symbol that continues the run advances it ($q_1\to q_3\to q_5$ on $0$, $q_2\to q_4\to q_5$ on $1$); a symbol that breaks the run starts a new run of length $1$ ($q_3,q_2\to$ via $1$ to $q_2$; $q_4,q_2\to$ via $0$ to $q_1$). $q_5$ is accepting and absorbing. Hence the DFA accepts exactly the strings containing three equal consecutive symbols, i.e. the substring $000$ or $111$.

cmimc-2016-power-s3-03a.title: Track progress towards 001
cmimc-2016-power-s3-03a.body: Use states $s_0$ (start), $s_1$ (read $0$), $s_2$ (read $00$), $s_3$ (read $001$, accepting) and a dead state $r$. Transitions: $s_0\xrightarrow{0}s_1$, $s_1\xrightarrow{0}s_2$, $s_2\xrightarrow{1}s_3$; every other transition (including everything out of $s_3$ and $r$) goes to $r$, which loops on $0,1$. Only the string $001$ ends in $s_3$.

cmimc-2016-power-s3-03b.title: Parity of length
cmimc-2016-power-s3-03b.body: Use two states $E$ (start, accepting) and $O$. Reading either letter swaps $E\leftrightarrow O$. After $k$ letters the DFA is in $E$ iff $k$ is even, so it accepts exactly the even-length strings (including the empty string).

cmimc-2016-power-s3-03c.title: Track the value mod 5
cmimc-2016-power-s3-03c.body:
Reading a bit $b$ after a prefix of value $v$ gives the value $2v+b$, so it suffices to remember $v\bmod5$. Use states $0,1,2,3,4$ and the transition $\delta(r,b)=(2r+b)\bmod5$: 

- state $0$: bit $0\to0$, bit $1\to1$; state $1$: $0\to2$, $1\to3$; state $2$: $0\to4$, $1\to0$; state $3$: $0\to1$, $1\to2$; state $4$: $0\to3$, $1\to4$.

The empty string must be rejected although its value is $0$, so add a separate non-accepting start state $s$ with $s\xrightarrow{0}0$ and $s\xrightarrow{1}1$ and never return to it. The only accepting state is $0$. This uses $6$ states; the whole reading is left-to-right, so five residue states suffice (reading right to left would need more).

cmimc-2016-power-s3-04.title: $k=5$ is forced
cmimc-2016-power-s3-04.body:
Let $s_n$ be the state after reading $0^n$, so $s_{n+1}=f(s_n)$ for a function $f$ on three states. $s_0$ is rejecting and $s_3$ accepting, so $s_0
e s_3$. The sequence $s_0,s_1,s_2,s_3$ takes values among three states, so it eventually becomes periodic with tail length $\mu$ and cycle length $\lambda$, $\mu+\lambda\le3$ (the number of distinct states visited). Since $s_3
e s_0$, $\mu\ge1$ or $\lambda
e3$: the cases are $\lambda=3$ ($\mu=0$, impossible because then $s_3=s_0$), $\lambda=1$ ($\mu\le2$) or $\lambda=2$ ($\mu\le1$). In both remaining cases $3\ge\mu$ and $5-3=2$ is a multiple of $\lambda$ ($\lambda\in\{1,2\}$), so $s_5=s_3$, which is accepting. Hence $0^5$ is always accepted.

cmimc-2016-power-s3-04.title: $k=4$ is not forced
cmimc-2016-power-s3-04.body:
Take states $q_0\to q_1\to q_2\to q_1$ on $0$ (and anything on $1$), with only $q_1$ accepting. It rejects $\varepsilon$, accepts $000$ ($q_0,q_1,q_2,q_1$) and rejects $0000$ (ends in $q_2$). So $k=4$ is not forced and the answer is $5$.

**Answer: 5** (a search over all 3-state DFAs confirms this)

cmimc-2016-power-s4-01.title: Build a trie DFA
cmimc-2016-power-s4-01.body:
Let $L$ be finite and $m$ the maximum length of a word in $L$. Build a DFA with one state for every string of length at most $m$ over the alphabet (the state records exactly what has been read so far), a transition from state $u$ on letter $a$ to state $ua$ when $|ua|\le m$, plus one dead state that absorbs everything longer than $m$. Make a state accepting iff its string belongs to $L$. This DFA accepts exactly $L$. Hence every finite language is regular.

**Answer: Yes**

cmimc-2016-power-s4-02a.title: Pigeonhole
cmimc-2016-power-s4-02a.body: If $k=n+1$ words are fed into a DFA with $n$ states, two of them end in the same state by the pigeonhole principle. With $k=n$ the $n$ words could all end in different states (if all $n$ states are reachable, there is a set of $n$ words ending in $n$ different states), so $k=n+1$ is the smallest value that works for every set.

cmimc-2016-power-s4-02b.title: Pigeonhole argument
cmimc-2016-power-s4-02b.body: Suppose $D$ decides $L$ and has $n$ states. Among the $n+1$ words $\varepsilon,0,0^2,\ldots,0^n$ two, $0^i$ and $0^j$ with $i<j$, end in the same state. A DFA is deterministic, so $0^is$ and $0^js$ end in the same state for every string $s$. Take $s=1^i$: then $0^i1^i\in L$ is accepted, so $0^j1^i$ must be accepted too; but $0^j1^i\notin L$ since $j\ne i$. This contradiction shows no such $D$ exists. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-03.title: Pigeonhole
cmimc-2016-power-s4-03.body: Suppose a DFA with $N$ states decides the language. Among the $N+1$ words $1^{2^0},1^{2^1},\ldots,1^{2^N}$, two, $1^{2^i}$ and $1^{2^j}$ with $i<j$, end in the same state. Then for every suffix $s$ the words $1^{2^i}s$ and $1^{2^j}s$ get the same verdict. Take $s=1^{2^i}$: $1^{2^i}s=1^{2^{i+1}}$ is in the language, but $1^{2^j}s=1^{2^j+2^i}$ has length strictly between $2^j$ and $2^{j+1}$, hence not a power of $2$, so it is not in the language. Contradiction. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-04a.title: Pigeonhole
cmimc-2016-power-s4-04a.body: Consider $q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_p$: these are $p+1$ states (the input is long enough, $n\ge p$), but $M$ only has $p$ states. By the pigeonhole principle two of them are equal: $q_i=q_j$ for some $0\le i<j\le p$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-04b.title: Check the three conditions
cmimc-2016-power-s4-04b.body:
$y=s_{i+1}\ldots s_j$ is nonempty since $i<j$, and $|xy|=j\le p=P$.

Let $\delta^*(q,w)$ denote the state reached from $q$ after reading $w$. Since $q_i=q_j$, we have $\delta^*(q_0,x)=q_i=q_j=\delta^*(q_0,xy)$, so $\delta^*(q_i,y)=q_i$. By induction on $k$, $\delta^*(q_0,xy^k)=q_i$ for all $k\ge0$ (for $k=0$ it is $\delta^*(q_0,x)=q_i$; if it holds for $k$ then $\delta^*(q_0,xy^{k+1})=\delta^*(q_i,y)=q_i$). Then $\delta^*(q_0,xy^kz)=\delta^*(q_i,z)=\delta^*(q_0,xyz)$, which is an accepting state since $xyz=s\in L$. So $xy^kz\in L$ for all $k\ge0$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-04c.title: Pump to a composite length
cmimc-2016-power-s4-04c.body: Suppose $L$ is regular with pumping length $P$. Choose a prime $q>P$ and a string $w\in L$ of length $q$ (e.g. $0^q$). Write $w=xyz$ as in the lemma, with $\ell=|y|\ge1$. Then $xy^iz\in L$ for every $i\ge0$, and $|xy^iz|=q+(i-1)\ell$. Take $i=q+1$: the length is $q+q\ell=q(1+\ell)$, with $q\ge2$ and $1+\ell\ge2$, which is not prime. So $xy^{q+1}z\notin L$, contradicting the lemma. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-05a.title: Flip the accepting states
cmimc-2016-power-s4-05a.body: Let $D=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$ decide $L$. Then $D'=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,Q\setminus F)$ follows exactly the same path on every word $w$. The word $w$ ends in a state of $Q\setminus F$ iff it ends outside $F$ iff $w\notin L$. So $D'$ accepts exactly $L^c$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-05b.title: Product automaton
cmimc-2016-power-s4-05b.body: Let $M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$ decide $A$ and $M'=(Q',\Sigma,\delta',q_0',F')$ decide $B$. Define $M''$ with states $Q\times Q'$, start $(q_0,q_0')$, transition $\delta''((q,q'),a)=(\delta(q,a),\delta'(q',a))$ and accepting set $F\times F'$. By induction on $|w|$, after reading $w$ the automaton $M''$ is in the state $(\delta^*(q_0,w),\delta'^*(q_0',w))$, i.e. the pair of states reached by $M$ and $M'$. Thus $M''$ accepts $w$ iff $M$ accepts $w$ and $M'$ accepts $w$, i.e. iff $w\in A\cap B$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-05c.title: Product automaton again
cmimc-2016-power-s4-05c.body: Use the same product DFA as for the intersection (states $Q\times Q'$, $\delta''((q,q'),a)=(\delta(q,a),\delta'(q',a))$, start $(q_0,q_0')$), but with accepting set $F''=\{(q,q'):q\in F\text{ or }q'\in F'\}$. After reading $w$ it is in the pair of states reached by $M$ and $M'$, which lies in $F''$ iff $M$ accepts or $M'$ accepts, i.e. iff $w\in A\cup B$. ∎ (Alternatively $A\cup B=(A^c\cap B^c)^c$, using the previous two parts.)

cmimc-2016-power-s4-05d.title: Combine closure results
cmimc-2016-power-s4-05d.body: $A\setminus B=A\cap B^c$. $B^c$ is regular by the complement result, and then $A\cap B^c$ is regular by the intersection result. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s4-06.title: Build a DFA for $L_0$ directly
cmimc-2016-power-s4-06.body:
Let $D=(Q,\{0,1\},\delta,q_0,F)$ decide $L$. Build $D_0$ with states: a start state $s$; states $(q,a)$ meaning "$D$ is in state $q$ after reading letters $a_1\ldots a_i$ with $a_i=a$, and the next input symbol is the check bit"; states $(q,a,t)$ meaning "the check bit $t$ was read, now expect $a_{i+1}$"; and a dead state. 

- From $s$, reading $a_1=a$ goes to $(\delta(q_0,a),a)$.
- From $(q,a)$, reading $t\in\{0,1\}$ goes to $(q,a,t)$.
- From $(q,a,t)$, reading $b$: if $t=1$ exactly when $a\ne b$, go to $(\delta(q,b),b)$; otherwise go to the dead state.
- Accepting states: $(q,a)$ with $q\in F$, and $s$ iff $q_0\in F$ (the empty word, $k=0$). The dead state loops.

By induction on the length, $D_0$ reaches $(q,a)$ after reading $a_1s_{1,2}a_2\ldots a_i$ exactly when all check bits were correct, with $q=\delta^*(q_0,a_1\ldots a_i)$ and $a=a_i$; any wrong check bit leads to the dead state. Hence $D_0$ accepts exactly the words of $L_0$, and $L_0$ is regular (it uses $2|Q|+4|Q|+2$ states, a finite number).

(The official solution writes $L_0=L_1\cap L_2$ with $L_1=\{a_1x_1a_2\ldots a_k:a_1\ldots a_k\in L\}$ and $L_2$ the set of words with correct check bits, both regular.)

**Answer: Yes**

cmimc-2016-power-s5-07.title: Identify the language
cmimc-2016-power-s5-07.body: Since every arrow reads either letter, the state depends only on the length $\ell$ of the input: $q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3$ for $\ell=0,1,2,3$, then $q_4,q_5,q_2,q_3,\ldots$ cycling. The accepting states $q_3$ (reached at lengths $3,7,11,\ldots$) and $q_5$ (lengths $5,9,13,\ldots$) together accept exactly the odd lengths $3,5,7,\ldots$, so $L$ is the set of strings of odd length at least $3$.

cmimc-2016-power-s5-07.title: Two modifications
cmimc-2016-power-s5-07.body:
1. State $q_4$ behaves exactly like $q_2$ (both reject and both lead to an accepting state next). Redirect the arrow $q_3\to q_4$ to $q_3\to q_2$ and delete $q_4$.
2. Now $q_5$ is unreachable, so delete it as well.

The result is $q_0\to q_1\to q_2\leftrightarrow q_3$ with $q_3$ accepting: $4$ states instead of $6$, still accepting exactly the odd lengths $\ge3$. It cannot be improved: the lengths $0$, $1$, even $\ge2$ and odd $\ge3$ lead to $4$ pairwise distinguishable classes, so $4$ states are needed.

cmimc-2016-power-s5-08.title: Seven states suffice
cmimc-2016-power-s5-08.body: States: $A_0,A_1,A_2$ for "only zeros read so far, $n\equiv i\pmod3$" (start $A_0$), $B_0,B_1,B_2$ for "a $1$ has been read; the current value of $n-m\equiv i\pmod3$", and a dead state $R$. Transitions: $A_i\xrightarrow{0}A_{i+1}$, $A_i\xrightarrow{1}B_{i-1}$, $B_i\xrightarrow{1}B_{i-1}$, $B_i\xrightarrow{0}R$, $R$ loops. Accepting states: $A_0$ and $B_0$. This decides $L$.

cmimc-2016-power-s5-08.title: Seven states are needed
cmimc-2016-power-s5-08.body:
Consider the seven words $0,00,000,1,11,111,10$. They are pairwise distinguishable, meaning that for any two of them some suffix is accepted after one and rejected after the other:

- $0^i$ and $0^j$ with $1\le i<j\le3$: use the suffix $0^{3-i}$; then $0^{3}\in L$ but $0^{j+3-i}\notin L$ since $j-i\not\equiv0\pmod 3$.
- $1^i$ and $1^j$ with $1\le i<j\le3$: use the suffix $1^{s}$ with $s\in\{0,1,2\}$ chosen so that $-i-s\equiv0\pmod3$; the other word then has $-j-s\not\equiv0$.
- $0^i$ and $1^j$: use a suffix $0^c$ with $i+c\equiv0\pmod3$, $c\ge1$: $0^{i+c}\in L$ but $1^j0^c\notin L$.
- $10$ and any of the other six: $10$ can never be extended into a word of $L$ (a $0$ after a $1$), whereas each of the other six words has an extension in $L$.

If a DFA had fewer than $7$ states, two of these words would end in the same state, and then every suffix would give the same verdict for both, contradicting distinguishability. So at least $7$ states are needed, and $7$ are enough.

**Answer: 7**

cmimc-2016-power-s5-09a.title: Count to $n$
cmimc-2016-power-s5-09a.body: Use states $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ where $p_i$ means "$i-1$ symbols have been read" (start $p_1$), with transition $p_i\to p_{i+1}$ on both $0$ and $1$ for $i<n$. From $p_n$, reading $1$ goes to an accepting sink $A$ and reading $0$ goes to a rejecting sink $R$; $A$ and $R$ loop on both symbols. The $n$-th symbol decides the outcome and nothing after it matters. This has $n+2$ states, so $c=2$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s5-09b.title: Distinguishable words
cmimc-2016-power-s5-09b.body: Let $D$ decide $\mathcal R_n$ and suppose it has fewer than $2^n$ states. There are $2^n$ binary words of length $n$, so two different ones, $u\ne v$, end in the same state. They differ at some position $i$ from the left ($1\le i\le n$), say $u_i=1$ and $v_i=0$. Append $0^{i-1}$ to both: in $u0^{i-1}$ the $i$-th symbol of $u$ is now $n$-th from the right and equals $1$, so $u0^{i-1}\in\mathcal R_n$; in $v0^{i-1}$ that symbol is $0$, so $v0^{i-1}\notin\mathcal R_n$. But $u$ and $v$ end in the same state, so $u0^{i-1}$ and $v0^{i-1}$ end in the same state and are both accepted or both rejected. Contradiction. Hence $D$ has at least $2^n$ states. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s5-10.title: No extension works
cmimc-2016-power-s5-10.body:
Every nonempty word of $L=\{0^n1^n\}$ starts with $0$, and $\varepsilon\in L$. A word $vw$ with $v=111100$ starts with $1$ and is nonempty, so it is never in $L$. Hence $S_{111100}(L)=\varnothing$.

**Answer: the empty set**

cmimc-2016-power-s5-11.title: Classes correspond to reachable states
cmimc-2016-power-s5-11.body:
Two strings are equivalent iff they end in the same state, so the equivalence classes correspond to the states that are reached by at least one string, namely the states reachable from the start state. There are at most $N$ of them.

Equality fails for a DFA with a state that is not reachable from the start state, for instance a two-state DFA over $\{0,1\}$ where both arrows from the start state $q_0$ loop back to $q_0$ and the second state $q_1$ has no incoming arrow: $\equiv_M$ has only one class.

cmimc-2016-power-s5-12.title: Same state, same future
cmimc-2016-power-s5-12.body: Let $x\equiv_My$, i.e. $\delta^*(q_0,x)=\delta^*(q_0,y)=:r$. For any $z\in\Sigma^*$, $\delta^*(q_0,xz)=\delta^*(r,z)=\delta^*(q_0,yz)$. Hence $xz\in A\iff\delta^*(r,z)\in F\iff yz\in A$. As this holds for all $z$, $S_x(A)=S_y(A)$, i.e. $x\equiv_Ay$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s5-13.title: Regular implies finitely many classes
cmimc-2016-power-s5-13.body: Let a DFA $M$ with state set $Q$ decide $A$. If $x\equiv_My$ then $x\equiv_Ay$ (previous problem), so each class of $\equiv_A$ is a union of classes of $\equiv_M$. Since $\equiv_M$ has at most $|Q|$ classes, $\equiv_A$ has at most $|Q|$ classes: finitely many.

cmimc-2016-power-s5-13.title: Finitely many classes implies regular
cmimc-2016-power-s5-13.body:
First, $\equiv_A$ is compatible with appending letters: if $x\equiv_Ay$ and $a\in\Sigma$ then $xa\equiv_Aya$, because $S_{xa}(A)=\{w:aw\in S_x(A)\}=\{w:aw\in S_y(A)\}=S_{ya}(A)$.

Let the classes be $T_1,\ldots,T_n$. Define a DFA with one state per class, start state the class $[\varepsilon]$, transition $\delta([v],a)=[va]$ (well defined by the compatibility), and accepting states the classes containing a word of $A$ (all words in a class agree on membership in $A$, since $\varepsilon\in S_v(A)\iff v\in A$). By induction on $|w|$, the DFA is in state $[w]$ after reading $w$. So it accepts $w$ iff $[w]$ is accepting iff $w\in A$. Hence $A$ is regular, and each state of this DFA is exactly one equivalence class of $\equiv_A$. ∎

cmimc-2016-power-s5-14.title: Run the algorithm
cmimc-2016-power-s5-14.body:
Accepting: $q_2,q_3,q_4$; non-accepting: $q_0,q_1,q_5$. First marks: all (accepting, non-accepting) pairs. Next round: $(q_0,q_5)$: on $1$ they go to $q_2$ and $q_5$ (a marked pair), so mark it; $(q_1,q_5)$: on $1$ they go to $q_3$ and $q_5$ (marked), so mark it. $(q_0,q_1)$: on $0$ they go to each other, on $1$ to $q_2,q_3$ (both accepting, unmarked): stays unmarked. Among accepting states: $(q_2,q_3)$: on $0$ both go to $q_4$, on $1$ both go to $q_5$: unmarked; $(q_2,q_4)$: on $0$ to $q_4,q_4$, on $1$ to $q_5,q_5$: unmarked; so $q_2\sim q_3\sim q_4$.

Merge $\{q_0,q_1\}$, $\{q_2,q_3,q_4\}$, $\{q_5\}$ to get the 3-state DFA described in the answer, which accepts exactly the strings with a single $1$ (i.e. $0^*10^*$).

cmimc-2016-power-s5-15.title: Marked means distinguishable
cmimc-2016-power-s5-15.body: Say states $Q_i,Q_j$ are *distinguishable* if some word $w$ leads one to an accepting state and the other to a non-accepting state. By induction on the length of the shortest distinguishing word, a pair is marked iff it is distinguishable: a pair is initially marked iff $w=\varepsilon$ distinguishes it, and if $aw$ distinguishes $(Q_i,Q_j)$ then $w$ distinguishes $(\delta(Q_i,a),\delta(Q_j,a))$, which is marked by induction, so $(Q_i,Q_j)$ gets marked (conversely a marked pair is distinguishable by the word that produced the mark). So unmarked pairs are exactly the pairs of states with the same future behaviour, and this is an equivalence relation, so merging is consistent with the transitions.

cmimc-2016-power-s5-15.title: Count with Myhill-Nerode
cmimc-2016-power-s5-15.body: Delete states unreachable from the start state. Every remaining state is reached by some word $x$, and two words $x,y$ reaching states $Q_i,Q_j$ satisfy $x\equiv_Ay$ iff $Q_i,Q_j$ are indistinguishable (their futures $S_x(A)$ and $S_y(A)$ are the sets of words accepted from $Q_i,Q_j$). Hence the states of the merged DFA correspond one-to-one to the classes of $\equiv_A$. By the Myhill-Nerode theorem every DFA deciding $A$ has at least as many states as there are classes of $\equiv_A$ (distinct classes need distinct states, by the first half of the proof of that theorem). So the merged DFA has the minimum number of states. ∎
